groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What is fed into the supercomputers?

evidence.summary: Supercomputers use large amounts of physical and chemical data to represent possible futures.

distractors.B: The description refers to huge amounts of two kinds of data, not just summer temperatures.
distractors.C: The input is described as physical and chemical data, not personal forecasts alone.

options.label: A
options.text: Physical and chemical data.

options.label: B
options.text: Only records of summer temperatures.

options.label: C
options.text: Only forecasts made by individual scientists.

questions.prompt: What does Marvel say a projection depends on?

evidence.summary: Marvel explains projections through an if-this-then-that relationship.

distractors.A: Her example is about future consequences rather than an event already completed.
distractors.B: She distinguishes a conditional projection from an unconditional statement of what will happen.

options.label: A
options.text: Whether the future has already happened.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether a prediction sounds likely.

options.label: C
options.text: What action is taken.

questions.prompt: What is identified as the main factor in climate change?

evidence.summary: Human activity and its greenhouse gas emissions are identified as the main factor.

distractors.A: Supercomputers are tools for modelling, not the main driver named.
distractors.C: The naming of models is not identified as a driver of climate change.

options.label: A
options.text: The number of available supercomputers.

options.label: B
options.text: Human activity, especially greenhouse gas emissions.

options.label: C
options.text: The names scientists give their models.

questions.prompt: Clouds can also warm the planet through their own {{blank}}.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which example follows Marvel's distinction between projection and prediction?

evidence.summary: A projection describes a conditional outcome rather than one inevitable future.

distractors.A: The condition is essential in Marvel's explanation of a projection.
distractors.B: She explicitly warns against treating model output as certainty.

options.label: A
options.text: One outcome will happen regardless of the choices made.

options.label: B
options.text: A possible outcome becomes certain because a computer produces it.

options.label: C
options.text: If a particular action is taken, a particular outcome follows.

questions.prompt: Which influence is singled out as especially important?

evidence.summary: The discussion singles out human activity, especially greenhouse gas emissions.

distractors.A: The number of named scenarios is not the causal factor given.
distractors.C: Reading speed is not identified as the main climate influence.

options.label: A
options.text: The number of modelled futures given a name.

options.label: B
options.text: Emissions caused by human activity.

options.label: C
options.text: The speed at which researchers read their results.

questions.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to describe clouds as having only a cooling effect?

evidence.summary: Clouds both block incoming sunlight and contribute a greenhouse warming effect.

distractors.B: The explanation does not restrict the cooling effect to summer.
distractors.C: Cloud effects are an additional modelling influence, not a replacement for greenhouse-gas modelling.

options.label: A
options.text: They also have a warming greenhouse effect.

options.label: B
options.text: They stop sunlight only in summer.

options.label: C
options.text: They remove the need to model greenhouse gases.

tests.title: Climate information: causes, uncertainty and choices

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: The temperature figure used to illustrate the UK record is {{blank}} degrees Celsius.

evidence.summary: The opening illustration uses a June record of thirty-seven point seven degrees Celsius.

evidence.summary: The introduction compares subsequent research with the one-point-five-degree target.

questions.prompt: The imbalance compares incoming solar energy with outgoing {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Outgoing radiation is the other quantity in the definition of the Earth's energy imbalance.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Two categories of input: physical and {{blank}} data.

evidence.summary: Chemical data are named alongside physical data as inputs to the models.

questions.prompt: Marvel's preferred term for model outputs: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Marvel distinguishes model projections from predictions.

questions.prompt: Key feature of such outputs: they are {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Marvel makes dependence on specified conditions central to a projection.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What do clouds block to produce cooling? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The cooling mechanism involves intercepting sunlight.

questions.prompt: What effect accounts for clouds also producing warming? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Marvel attributes the warming side to the clouds' own greenhouse effect.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What do the presenters' questions emphasise about accurate modelling?

evidence.summary: The two questions focus on tracking changing clouds and obtaining sufficient worldwide information.

distractors.A: Pippa explicitly asks about information from around the world.
distractors.C: Movement is presented as a complication, not a way of reducing data needs.

options.label: A
options.text: Global information is irrelevant when a model uses a supercomputer.

options.label: B
options.text: Both a changing subject and a large information requirement make it demanding.

options.label: C
options.text: The models need fewer data once clouds start moving.

questions.prompt: Why does Marvel still support scientific modelling despite the difficulty?

evidence.summary: Modelling is defended as necessary to understand and adapt to a changing climate.

distractors.B: The discussion explicitly excludes no climate change as an option.
distractors.C: Conditional projections preserve the importance of human choices.

options.label: A
options.text: Understanding the direction of unavoidable change is needed for adaptation.

options.label: B
options.text: A model can promise that no climate change will occur.

options.label: C
options.text: A model removes the need to make choices about emissions.

tests.title: Projections and decisions: interpreting conditional evidence

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: Reported UK June record used in the introduction: {{blank}} degrees Celsius.

evidence.summary: The temperature figure is a June record, not the global warming limit discussed next.

questions.prompt: Year in which the warming-limit agreement was reached: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The introduction dates the target-setting COP21 agreement to twenty fifteen.

questions.prompt: Incoming component of the energy comparison: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The imbalance compares incoming solar energy with outgoing radiation, rather than comparing two surface temperatures.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion mistakes a model's projection for an unconditional prediction?

evidence.summary: The warning is against treating a conditional projection as an inevitable outcome independent of action.

distractors.A: The data-based representation of possible futures is stated in the introduction to models.
distractors.C: Conditional outcomes are exactly the distinction Marvel makes.

options.label: A
options.text: The output can represent several possible futures informed by data.

options.label: B
options.text: The computer output identifies one future that must occur whatever people do.

options.label: C
options.text: The output can describe an outcome under specified actions.

questions.prompt: Why is human activity relevant to the conditional nature of the models?

evidence.summary: The models' dependence on other factors includes the human activities that drive emissions.

distractors.B: Human activity is explicitly included as a main influence, not omitted to create conditionality.
distractors.C: The measurement unit is explained separately from the causal influences.

options.label: A
options.text: Different actions and emissions are among the factors on which the projected future depends.

options.label: B
options.text: A projection becomes conditional only when human emissions are left out.

options.label: C
options.text: Human activity determines the unit in which energy imbalance is expressed.

questions.prompt: Which assumption is challenged by the explanation of clouds?

evidence.summary: The dual effect means blocking incoming sunlight and contributing warming can coexist.

distractors.A: Multiple effects are the explanation, not the assumption being challenged.
distractors.B: The cloud greenhouse effect supports, rather than challenges, considering greenhouse mechanisms.

options.label: A
options.text: That clouds can influence the climate in more than one way.

options.label: B
options.text: That greenhouse effects need to be considered in climate models.

options.label: C
options.text: That a feature which blocks sunlight cannot also contribute to warming.

evidence.summary: Trapping heat is the presenter’s restatement of the warming mechanism.

evidence.summary: The phrase characterises a system that is not in balance or functioning properly.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

evidence.summary: Jackson identifies adaptation as the reason to understand the direction of change.

evidence.summary: The presenter says that no climate change at all is not an option, rather than saying all responses are unavailable.

tests.title: Climate reasoning: distinguishing uncertainty from inaction

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What outgoing quantity is compared with energy arriving from the Sun? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The definition compares incoming solar energy with radiation leaving the Earth system.

questions.prompt: What kind of data is mentioned in addition to physical data? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The modelling inputs include chemical data as well as physical data.

questions.prompt: What equipment turns these large data inputs into representations of possible futures? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The recording describes supercomputers processing large datasets to depict possible futures.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Marvel says models produce {{blank}}, rather than predictions.

evidence.summary: Her distinction names the outputs projections because they depend on conditions.

questions.prompt: A future outcome specified with an if-clause is {{blank}} in Marvel's explanation.

evidence.summary: She illustrates conditionality with an if-action-then-outcome formulation.

questions.prompt: Within human activity, the main influence singled out is greenhouse gas {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The description specifically highlights greenhouse gas emissions as a human influence.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Incoming energy blocked in the cooling mechanism: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The account attributes the cooling side to blocked sunlight rather than the trapping of outgoing heat.

questions.prompt: Mechanism responsible for the opposite effect: the clouds' own {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The warming side is attributed to a greenhouse effect of clouds.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What do the presenters' concerns establish about the models?

evidence.summary: Their concerns identify practical demands without overturning the stated conditional nature of models.

distractors.B: The questions describe difficulties, not proof of uselessness.
distractors.C: Earlier reasoning explicitly distinguishes projections from guarantees.

options.label: A
options.text: Accurate projections require tracking changing conditions and sufficient information.

options.label: B
options.text: The existence of moving clouds proves that conditional models cannot be useful.

options.label: C
options.text: The amount of global information turns projections into guaranteed predictions.

questions.prompt: How does Jackson's point connect to Marvel's answer?

evidence.summary: The exchange links the practical need to adapt with Marvel's support for scientific work.

distractors.A: Marvel explicitly supports doing science because some change is unavoidable in this account.
distractors.B: The discussion defends models despite their conditional nature, not only after a guaranteed prediction exists.

options.label: A
options.text: Science is unnecessary because adaptation means avoiding any climate change.

options.label: B
options.text: A definite prediction is required before conditional projections can have any role.

options.label: C
options.text: Knowing the trajectory helps adaptation, so the lack of a no-change option supports doing science.

sourceReview.method: Official BBC transcript meaning cross-checked with the direct lesson recording; word-timed ASR used only to locate passages.
